case_study_insert.main_stem: Orchardale Beverages (OBV) is a public limited company in the fruit-drink manufacturing sector, based in the Campania region and employing a workforce of 110. Founded in 2006 by Sofia Marchetti, it supplies cold-pressed juice to cafes and supermarkets and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. OBV plans to invest $1,150,000 in a new bottling and cold-press line, financed by $500,000 venture capital and $650,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $5 a unit and a selling price of $13, and produces 150,000 units a year. OBV faces fruit-waste losses of 5% of input and quality complaints about sediment in its juice.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research and Operations Summary — Q2 2025: The cold-press line bottled 33,000 litres in the quarter, with a defect rate of 1.9% against 3.4% a year earlier. Complaints fell from 52 to 29 a month. Average delivery to cafes was 2.4 days. A survey of 1,200 shoppers found 66% would pay $0.35 more for cold-pressed juice and 59% check the label for added sugar. Fruit waste was 5% of input. A training check shows 22 of 110 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new filler; off-the-job training at the industry college costs $720 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Orchardale Beverages as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Beverage Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.0% from $13.15 to $14.07 an hour, lifting bottling-floor wages. (3) Fruit and glass-bottle input costs have risen 11.5% year-on-year, while consumer spending on healthy drinks grew 5.6%.

questions.question_text: OBV is funding its $1,150,000 bottling and cold-press line with $500,000 venture capital and $650,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for OBV of using retained profit rather than more venture capital.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no share of ownership to be given away and no dividend obligation, so Sofia Marchetti's existing shareholders keep more control of the $1,150,000 cold-press line. Venture capital would demand an equity stake and likely a return, whereas the $650,000 retained profit can absorb the 11.5% rise in fruit and glass costs without diluting ownership.

Point 2: Retained profit has no repayment schedule, protecting cash flow against fixed costs of $420,000 a year while the new line is commissioned. Venture capital can also bring useful expertise, but its investors may push for quicker returns; using internally generated funds lets OBV respond to the 66% of 1,200 shoppers willing to pay $0.35 more for cold-pressed juice at its own pace.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to OBV's financing decision.

questions.question_text: OBV is launching its new cold-pressed juice range to cafes. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should OBV choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: TV gives OBV rapid mass reach and can show the cold-press process to millions, supporting the 66% of 1,200 shoppers who would pay $0.35 more. However, airtime is expensive for a company with $420,000 fixed costs and a $1,150,000 line to fund, and many viewers are outside the cafe distribution network, so a large part of the budget is wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheaper and reaches the local catchment around OBV's Campania cafes, and short messages can announce the launch economically. Its weakness is that audio cannot show the juice or communicate the 59% of shoppers who check labels for added sugar, and the area reached is too small to support 150,000 units of output.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and wellness influencers can show the cold-pressed product and its label directly to health-conscious buyers, with engagement tracked against the 33,000 litres bottled last quarter. Results build gradually and depend on credible partners, but cost per reached shopper is low and the content can answer the 29 monthly complaints about the product.

Recommendation: OBV should choose social media influencer marketing, with small cafe tasting events. It targets the segment already identified in the survey, shows the product that radio cannot, and costs far less than television. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a $1,150,000 investment; radio is rejected as too narrow for a brand supplying cafes and supermarkets beyond one locality.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to OBV.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of OBV with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: OBV faces quality complaints about sediment and 5% fruit waste under laissez-faire leadership. Explain two benefits for OBV of introducing team working in its workforce of 110.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working brings operators together to share check routines on the new filler, which can reduce the 1.9% defect rate and address the complaints about sediment. In a laissez-faire setting where staff receive little direction, teams create shared responsibility, so the 5% fruit waste is more likely to be cut and the 59% of 1,200 shoppers checking labels see a consistent product.

Point 2: Working in teams raises support and morale, helping retain the 110 staff and reducing the need to train the 22 of 110 still missing on-the-job training at $720 each. Better coordination also protects the 2.4-day delivery record to cafes, so the $1,150,000 bottling line can meet demand for the juice that 66% of shoppers would pay $0.35 more for.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to OBV's complaints, waste, delivery and expansion.

questions.question_text: OBV must train 22 of 110 staff who have not completed on-the-job training on the new filler. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the industry college. Which should OBV choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the filler is tailored to OBV's own bottling settings and hygiene rules, costs no course fees, and keeps the 22 trainees productive during the 33,000-litre quarter. It can directly reduce the 1.9% defect rate and the 5% fruit waste because supervisors correct technique at once. Drawbacks are that busy operators have limited time to teach, bad habits can spread, and there is no external certificate for cafe buyers.

Off-the-job training: The industry college course at $720 per employee costs 22 × $720 = $15,840, small relative to the $1,150,000 investment. It gives structured food-safety skills and a recognised certificate, useful for supplying cafes and supermarkets. However, it removes 22 of 110 staff from the line during production, risking deliveries longer than 2.4 days, and generic content will still need adaptation to OBV's cold-press equipment.

Decision: OBV should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, adding short certified college modules later. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids disrupting output while quality complaints about sediment persist. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because the lost shifts and $15,840 fee would hit the 33,000-litre quarter and the generic course would not cover the new filler's exact settings. A pilot on one shift should compare the 1.9% defect rate and 5% waste before OBV spends $15,840 on all 22 staff.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to OBV.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of OBV.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how OBV's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ ($13.00 − $5.00) = $420,000 ÷ $8.00 = 52,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 52,500 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Calculate OBV's average total cost per litre.
sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Average total cost = Fixed cost per unit + Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ 150,000 units = $2.80, plus $5.00 = $7.80. Answer: average total cost is $7.80 a litre.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways OBV's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 52,500-unit break-even with output of 150,000 litres gives a margin of safety of 97,500 units, showing how much demand can fall before losses and guiding use of the $1,150,000 cold-press line.
2. Contribution per unit of $8.00 (from $13.00 − $5.00) lets managers test a cafe discount: cutting the $13.00 price by $1 to $12.00 leaves $7.00 contribution, so they can weigh extra volume against the 29 monthly complaints about value.
3. Average total cost of $7.80 against the $13.00 price gives a $5.20 margin a litre, a benchmark for the 5% fruit-waste reduction target and for deciding whether to accept the $0.35 premium mentioned by 66% of shoppers.
4. Managers can compare unit cost with the $720 per-employee training fee and 22 untrained staff to judge whether cutting the 1.9% defect rate is worth the spend, and renegotiate the $5.00 variable cost given 11.5% fruit and glass inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 52,500 units | (ii) Average total cost = $7.80 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 97,500-unit safety margin versus 150,000 litres; discount pricing from $13.00 against $8.00 contribution; $7.80 cost versus $13.00 price and 5% waste; and $720 training spend benchmark against 22 untrained staff.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate OBV's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has OBV's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.84 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.04 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.29 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $160,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $460,000; 2025 current assets = $180,000 + $195,000 + $115,000 = $490,000. For 2024, $460,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.84 and ($460,000 − $210,000) ÷ $250,000 = $250,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.00. For 2025, $490,000 ÷ $240,000 = 2.04 and ($490,000 − $180,000) ÷ $240,000 = $310,000 ÷ $240,000 = 1.29.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. The first ratio rose from 1.84 to 2.04 because current liabilities fell from $250,000 to $240,000 while current assets grew from $460,000 to $490,000, helped by cash rising from $90,000 to $115,000. The second measure improved from 1.00 to 1.29; excluding inventories, it shows OBV can cover short-term debts from liquid assets alone, valuable while $500,000 of venture capital and a $1,150,000 bottling line are being absorbed. The caution is trade receivables, up from $160,000 to $195,000, which tie up cash if cafe customers pay late, and inventories have fallen to $180,000, so stock cover for the new juice launch should be monitored.

Conclusion: OBV's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the improvement is not dependent on stock, so short-term solvency is stronger. Rising receivables are the main residual risk, so OBV should tighten credit control as the cold-press line ramps up.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

questions.question_text: OBV is considering a new juice with no added sugar. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for OBV of this product change.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A no-added-sugar juice directly matches the 59% of 1,200 surveyed shoppers who check labels for added sugar and supports the 66% who would pay $0.35 more for cold-pressed juice. It can help answer the 29 monthly complaints and protect the $8.00 contribution per litre against 11.5% fruit and glass inflation, strengthening the case for the $1,150,000 line.

Disadvantage: Reformulation may raise the $5.00 variable cost if fruit content must increase, squeezing the $7.80 average total cost advantage, and the insert gives no figure for recipe or relabelling cost, so the net effect cannot be quantified. A new taste may also disappoint existing cafe buyers, risking the 33,000-litre quarterly baseline and the 2.4-day delivery routine. OBV should test the recipe with a small cafe group before a full launch.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to OBV's survey, cost data and complaints.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 7.0% minimum wage increase and the 11.5% rise in fruit and glass-bottle input costs will affect OBV. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): Higher rates make borrowing and venture-capital-backed expansion more expensive for OBV. The insert does not state that the $500,000 venture capital carries interest, so no interest saving can be computed; if any future borrowing were variable-rate, the extra 0.75 percentage point would apply to the amount borrowed. Against fixed costs of $420,000, the direct effect on current operations is limited, though it may slightly slow the 5.6% growth in healthy-drink spending.

Minimum wage increase (7.0%, to $14.07 an hour): OBV's workforce of 110 includes hourly-paid bottling staff, so payroll rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual wage total would be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 150,000 units ÷ 110 staff = about 1,363.6 litres per worker, so the rise is affordable only if that rate holds; training the 22 untrained staff and cutting the 5% fruit waste would help.

Input cost inflation (11.5%): Fruit and glass bottles feed the $5.00 variable cost on every litre. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the full $5.00 were exposed, 11.5% × $5.00 = $0.575, about $0.58 a litre, and at 150,000 units that is roughly $86,250 a year (150,000 × $0.575). Even a smaller exposed share reduces the $8.00 contribution on every litre and recurs with each unit sold.

Conclusion: The 11.5% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It repeats across 150,000 litres and directly erodes the contribution that funds the $1,150,000 bottling line, whereas the interest effect on existing operations is limited and the wage rise can be offset by sustaining 1,363.6 litres per worker. OBV should cut the 5% waste and use the $0.35 premium accepted by 66% of shoppers rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to OBV.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on OBV's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
